clue.text: Hence cast for production of The Rake's Progress ?

definitions.meaning: a cast is made from a hollow form into which molten metal or plaster is poured
what a garden rake progressively produces is fine loose topsoil

explanation.surface: A theatre company casts its staging of Stravinsky's opera The Rake's Progress.
explanation.walkthrough: The Rake's Progress looks like the opera or Hogarth's prints; here the rake is the garden tool, and its work leaves crumbly soil, which gardeners call by the same word as the caster's form.
explanation.definitionFit: The same word names the hollow form a casting comes from and the loose crumbly earth a raked bed yields.

clue.text: Incredible doings here on Dec 24, said Brooke

definitions.text: Incredible doings here on Dec 24, said Brooke

parts.words: Incredible doings here on Dec 24, said Brooke
parts.note: Rupert Brooke's poem The Old Vicarage, Grantchester mocks villages near Cambridge, one for unbelievable deeds on Christmas Eve

explanation.walkthrough: In The Old Vicarage, Grantchester Rupert Brooke writes 'things are done you'd not believe' at this village near Cambridge 'on Christmas Eve'.
explanation.definitionFit: A village outside Cambridge which Brooke's poem accuses of unbelievable goings-on on Christmas Eve.

clue.text: The habitué's drink

parts.note: a regular at a pub orders the same thing every time and asks for it by that name

explanation.walkthrough: A regular customer in a bar simply asks for 'the usual', the drink the barman knows they always have.
explanation.definitionFit: A regular customer's habitual order is the customary one, asked for in two words.

clue.text: Silent pictures put on of the Oaks

parts.note: dumb means unable or unwilling to speak
paintings and pictures make up art
taken as written

explanation.surface: Silent films being shown about the Oaks horse race.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silent pictures' suggests old films, and the Oaks a horse race; it is Dumbarton Oaks, the Washington estate where the 1944 conference planned the United Nations.
explanation.definitionFit: The name completes Dumbarton Oaks, the Washington mansion that gave its name to a 1944 conference.

clue.text: Some felines and canines are so composed

definitions.text: Some felines and canines are so composed

parts.words: Some felines and canines are so composed
parts.note: when it rains cats and dogs, those cats and dogs are made of what falls from the clouds

explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'raining cats and dogs' means pouring with rain, so the cats and dogs of that downpour consist of rain.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain that has fallen is the stuff the proverbial cats and dogs of a downpour consist of.

clue.text: Comes back to John Anderson in harness

indicators.note: the man's name is placed within the word for harness

parts.note: reins are the straps of a horse's harness
Burns's song begins 'John Anderson, my jo', jo meaning sweetheart

explanation.surface: A man returns to John Anderson to be back in his working harness.
explanation.walkthrough: Burns's poem 'John Anderson, my jo' supplies JO (Scots for sweetheart), which goes 'in' REINS.
explanation.definitionFit: To retort or reply is to come back at someone, the legal and literary sense of answering.

clue.text: Dizzy, loses his head, the Levantine

indicators.note: the man's surname drops its first letter

parts.note: Dizzy was the nickname of the Victorian prime minister Benjamin Disraeli

explanation.surface: A giddy man loses his head over someone from the eastern Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dizzy' looks like giddiness, but it was Benjamin Disraeli's nickname; 'loses his head' removes his D.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of the modern state on the eastern Mediterranean shore, the Levant.

clue.text: Ralph, take up law and act

indicators.note: in a down clue taking up the word law lifts it, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: to do is to act or perform

explanation.surface: A man named Ralph is told to study law and take action.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'take up' means read upwards. Ralph is the American essayist Ralph Waldo Emerson, so the definition is the name that follows Ralph.
explanation.definitionFit: Ralph Waldo Emerson's middle name follows Ralph, so it partners that first name.

clue.text: A cheat not only at the bridge table

definitions.text: A cheat not only at the bridge table

parts.words: A cheat not only at the bridge table
parts.note: a swindler, and also at cards a player who takes tricks

explanation.walkthrough: At bridge you win tricks, so a player taking them could be called a trick-ster; away from cards the word means a swindler.
explanation.definitionFit: A swindler who plays tricks on people, and also, at cards, a winner of tricks.

clue.text: Rosy like a fish ?

definitions.meaning: resembling the rudd, a red-finned freshwater fish, with the adjective ending -y

explanation.walkthrough: The rudd is a European freshwater fish with red fins, so 'like a rudd' makes the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A reddish, flushed complexion; read as rudd plus -y it also means resembling the red-finned rudd.

clue.text: Officer of the beat ?

parts.note: a beat suggests a police constable's round, but here it is the rhythm a marching band keeps

explanation.walkthrough: 'Officer of the beat' suggests a policeman on his round; the beat is musical, and the officer leads a marching band.
explanation.definitionFit: The leader of a military marching band, who sets its pace with a mace, holds this title.

clue.text: Pre-decimal financial inflation, Great Scot !

parts.note: L for pounds, from the old British money of pounds, shillings and pence (£sd)
inflating a tyre or balloon fills it with air
D for pence, from the old British money of pounds, shillings and pence (£sd)

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise at how prices rose before Britain went decimal.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British money was pounds, shillings and pence, written £sd with L and D; those two letters go round AIR. 'Great Scot!' is an exclamation, but here it is a great man of Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish landowner of an estate is a man of standing, a great Scotsman.

clue.text: Australian club cut by 50 per cent to streamline

indicators.note: the club's doubled name loses one of its two equal halves

parts.note: the ...-... is an Aboriginal Australian hardwood club

explanation.surface: An Australian sports club halves its staff to become more efficient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Streamline' looks like a verb about efficiency; read it as stream line, the course of a stream. A nulla (or nullah) is a watercourse or ravine, a word from India.
explanation.definitionFit: A watercourse or dry stream bed, the line a stream follows, is called by this Anglo-Indian word.

clue.text: Puck looks slippy to help make this match

definitions.text: Puck looks slippy to help make this match

parts.words: Puck looks slippy to help make this match
parts.note: Puck suggests Shakespeare's sprite, but it is the rubber disc slid across a frozen rink in a team game

explanation.walkthrough: Puck the fairy from A Midsummer Night's Dream is the misdirection; the puck is the disc in a sport played on a slippery frozen surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A team sport played on skates with sticks and a rubber puck on a frozen rink.

clue.text: Real reverse and setback for a Danish Francophil

indicators.note: the word real is written from its end back to its start

parts.note: read as set back, the word set turned round

explanation.surface: A genuine reversal and a setback for a Danish lover of France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reverse' turns REAL into LAER, and 'setback' read as 'set back' turns SET into TES. In Hamlet, Polonius's son is a Dane who longs to return to France.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonius's son in Hamlet is a Danish courtier who keeps asking leave to go back to Paris.

clue.text: Not Havelock's home. Robbie's

parts.note: the name suggests the land of the writer Havelock Ellis, but it was Robert Burns's farm

explanation.walkthrough: The name looks like Havelock Ellis's land, after the sexologist; in fact it is the farm near Dumfries where Robert Burns lived from 1788.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Burns farmed this estate near Dumfries, whose name looks like the land of Havelock Ellis.

clue.text: Hands us our cards — on dismissal? On the contrary

definitions.text: Hands us our cards — on dismissal? On the contrary

parts.words: Hands us our cards — on dismissal? On the contrary
parts.note: being handed your cards means being sacked; the contrary is being handed cards that ask you in

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain an employee 'given their cards' is dismissed; the opposite is handing out cards that ask people to come, such as invitations to a party.
explanation.definitionFit: Sending someone a written card asking them to an event is the opposite of sending them packing.

clue.text: The gambling majority once

parts.note: twenty-one, formerly the age of legal adulthood, is also a card game

explanation.walkthrough: Majority (legal adulthood) was once reached at 21; the French for twenty-one names a card game, the forerunner of blackjack.
explanation.definitionFit: A card game whose French name means twenty-one, the old age of coming of age.

clue.text: Eve's arrival not the main concern?

definitions.text: Eve's arrival not the main concern?

parts.words: Eve's arrival not the main concern?
parts.note: Genesis has Eve made from Adam's rib, so she came out of his flank; also a matter of lesser importance

explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis Eve is made from Adam's rib, so she issued from his side; the phrase also means a secondary matter.
explanation.definitionFit: A matter of secondary importance; read literally, offspring that came out of a flank, as Eve did from Adam.

clue.text: Let there be no delay to upset her

indicators.note: upsetting the words knocks their letters into a new order

explanation.surface: A command that there must be no delay, so as not to annoy a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to upset' rearranges NO DELAY into the girl's name; 'Let there be' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's given name, so a female person referred to as her.

clue.text: Three directions around the Persian coastline for swallows

indicators.note: the three compass letters are placed on both sides of the sea's name

parts.note: E, N and S are compass abbreviations for east, north and south
the Persian Gulf, the sea bounded by Iran and Arabia

explanation.surface: Swallows migrating along three compass routes round the shores of the Persian Gulf.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallows' looks like the birds, but it is the verb; 'around' puts E, N, S about GULF.
explanation.definitionFit: To swallow up something is to overwhelm or devour it completely.

clue.text: A number of old county families

definitions.meaning: an old subdivision of an English county

explanation.walkthrough: The old English shires were divided into districts called hundreds, said to have held a hundred families or hides.
explanation.definitionFit: The figure ten times ten also named a medieval division of an English shire.

clue.text: So far as I can see

definitions.text: So far as I can see

parts.words: So far as I can see
parts.note: the phrase usually means in my opinion, but read literally it is the limit of vision

explanation.walkthrough: The everyday phrase means 'in my opinion'; taken literally it is the line where sky meets land, the limit of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: The line where earth and sky appear to meet marks the farthest distance one can look.

clue.text: Telecommunicator

parts.note: tele- means far off, so one who carries word over a distance

explanation.walkthrough: The word suggests a telephone engineer, but tele- just means at a distance: someone who carries news.
explanation.definitionFit: A courier or herald communicates from afar by carrying the message in person.

clue.text: Wrong sex for hatter's confession

parts.note: a hatter, proverbially insane, might own up to being out of his mind; spaced differently, the same letters are a courteous way to address a lady

explanation.walkthrough: 'As mad as a hatter' is the British saying, so the hatter's confession is that he is mad. The same five letters also address a woman, the wrong sex for Lewis Carroll's Hatter.
explanation.definitionFit: A polite form of address for a woman, which spaced out reads as a madman's admission.

clue.text: Crowd actor in a Wessex tragedy

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A film extra appearing in one of Thomas Hardy's tragic Wessex novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' says the answer sits within 'Wessex tragedy'; Wessex suggests Thomas Hardy, whose novels are set there.
explanation.definitionFit: A film or stage performer hired to fill out a crowd scene, without lines.

clue.text: You all sound like a lot of hooters

indicators.note: the clue says the answer is heard as the sound of the horns

parts.note: many horns hooting make a tooty noise

explanation.surface: A crowd of people sounding like a load of car horns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound like' points to the noise of many hooters (horns), tooty, which is said like the Italian musical term for all players together.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian musical direction meaning everyone plays, literally 'all' addressed to the whole ensemble.

clue.text: Decimal alternative note-issuer

parts.note: decimal counting is based on ten
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A banknote issued by a bank as a decimal alternative to old currency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'note-issuer' suggests a bank printing banknotes; it is a singer producing musical notes.
explanation.definitionFit: A male singer of the high voice part issues musical notes when he sings.

clue.text: Gave a hand to reorganize the river depository

indicators.note: reorganizing the word puts its letters in a fresh order

parts.note: a delta is the fan of silt a river deposits at its mouth

explanation.surface: Someone helped to reorganize the storehouse by the river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reorganize' rearranges DELTA, the silt a river deposits at its mouth. 'Gave a hand' is not helping but handing out cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A card player who distributed a hand of cards to each player did so as the dealer.

clue.text: Are they slow to come to grips with fuel supplies?

definitions.text: Are they slow to come to grips with fuel supplies?

parts.words: Are they slow to come to grips with fuel supplies?
parts.note: a pair of extending grippers seen as idle, used to pick up coal

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests sluggish workers; the device is a scissor-jointed pair of tongs for reaching things such as lumps of coal without getting up.
explanation.definitionFit: Extending lattice tongs let a person reach and grip things, like coal, without moving from their chair.

clue.text: It sheds light on Englishmen's liability to hydrophobia

definitions.text: It sheds light on Englishmen's liability to hydrophobia

parts.words: It sheds light on Englishmen's liability to hydrophobia
parts.note: Noel Coward's song says only mad dogs and Englishmen go out at noon, and hydrophobia is rabies

explanation.walkthrough: Noel Coward's song 'Mad Dogs and Englishmen' says they go out in the noonday heat; hydrophobia is an old name for rabies, the madness of dogs.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel Coward's song claims only mad dogs and Englishmen venture out under the noon glare.

clue.text: This man comes from the North East and not another direction.

definitions.text: This man comes from the North

parts.note: nor means and not, joining negatives
S for south, a compass point other than north and east
E is the compass abbreviation for east

explanation.surface: A man claims to come from the north-east and from no other compass point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North East' looks like one compass point; the definition ends at North, and East supplies the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scandinavian of old, from Norway or the northern lands, is a man from the north.
